newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Boutros-Ghali cites progress in U.N. reform.
newsitem.headline: Boutros-Ghali cites progress in U.N. reform.

text.p: Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, in his annual report on Monday on the work of the United Nations, focused heavily on progress in carrying out reforms -- lack of which the United States has repeatedly cited in opposing his candidacy for re-election.

"This report details my ongoing effort at the managerial level towards a mission-driven, result-oriented organisation, showing enhanced performance, improved productivity and increased cost-effectiveness," Boutros-Ghali wrote.
"Reform efforts in the past year have shown us the future of the organisation. It is in essence a simple vision -- a vision of a United Nations that works."
When the United States announced in June that it would block a second five-year term for the veteran Egyptian diplomat, White House spokesman Mike McCurry zeroed in on the reform issue.

"We think there are most likely other people in the world who would be more capable of pursuing the (necessary) type of U.N. reform agenda," McCurry said. "That building is stuffed with too many bureaucrats and stuffed with too much waste and inefficiency."

The 157-page report, covering all aspects of U.N. operations from peacekeeping to development and from disarmament to humanitarian activities, was issued in advance of the annual General Assembly session opening on Tuesday.
A key issue to be decided during the session is who will lead the United Nations when Boutros-Ghali's current five-year term expires at the end of this year.

"The pages of this report depict a United Nations in the midst of a dramatic transformation," Boutros-Ghali wrote in the concluding section of his document. Although the transformation, which began at the end of the Cold War, had been neither smooth nor easy, and expectations for the United Nations were too high at the outset, the organisation had "moved definitively forward," he said.

"The structures of the United Nations are being streamlined and opened, the organisation streamlined and deregulated, costs reduced, accountability strengthened and performance improved. In the past five years alone, the distance travelled has been great," Boutros-Ghali added, alluding to the period during which he has been at the helm.

He outlined a blueprint for future improvements, saying: "The simplification of secretariat structures that I have introduced ... has paved the way for a further reorganization at the secretariat level..."
The guiding principle of his initiatives would continue to be "simplification and consolidation ... to eliminate duplication in support services and overlap in activities," he added.
